newsitem.title: CHINA: HK govt caution on new airport fees annoys agents.
newsitem.headline: HK govt caution on new airport fees annoys agents.

text.p: Government indecision over Hong Kong's new airport is threatening to drive away jobs and investment, said the Hong Kong Association of Freight Forwarding Agents (HAFFA).

In a statement, HAFFA, which represents 261 companies handling 90 percent of all of Hong Kong's outbound air cargo, said its greatest concern was predicted high fees at Chek Lap Kok airport, due to open next April.

Bridge toll charges, high rents, increased terminal and airline handling charges and higher travel to work costs for employees are also "likely to take their toll", HAFFA said. A precise fee structure is still being finalised, HAFFA added.
"If the proposed charges are implemented unchanged, the all-out efforts of HAFFA members to develop the air cargo industry over the last two decades will be severely wasted," said the association.

"Member agents may seriously consider relocating up to 30 percent of their operations to alternative sites in Taiwan, Shenzhen or Macau, resulting in loss of jobs and income in Hong Kong," the statement said.

HAFFA and Hong Kong Air Cargo Terminals Ltd (HACTL) have also made a joint appeal to retain HACTL's highly automated Terminal 2 building at Kai Tak as an alternative downtown centre for forwarders who cannot afford the move to the new airport.
"Regretfully, HAFFA has still to receive the government's reply on this matter," the HAFFA statement added.

"Whether the answer lies in the provision of special permits for the use of the Lantau link (to Chep Lap Kok) for HAFFA members or local transport companies, a ceiling on airport charges or the continuation of Terminal 2 to reduce costs for small shipments -- or a combination of all three, HAFFA believes decisions must be made," it said.
The statement urged proposed charges to be reconsidered, confirmed and made available so Hong Kong's freight forwarding agents can plan ahead for the future.
The Hong Kong government has so far declined to comment.
